Gaza Parkour

By: Paula Slier | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
In Gaza, youngsters are leaping high and reaching new heights - but not of the kind you might think ....

Summary:
Parkour, also known as “free running,” is popular among youngsters in Gaza. They say it gives them "a sense of freedom". They practice their sport in the graveyard, on the roofs of buildings and on the beach - we will film in all these locations. For youngsters who might otherwise not have much to do, the sport is a form of release and inspiration. Ahmed Matar heads the Gaza Parkour team that is affiliated with the WFPF - World Freerunning & Parkour Federation. Born 1996, he comes from Khan Younis in southern Gaza. He and his friends will take us on some terrifying flips and turns.
To not politicise the story, the questions we'll ask Ahmad and his friends will be about their love of the sport, why they do it, where they do it etc. Visually, a very strong colour piece.

Press Release:


Gaza’s Free-runners
It’s the ultimate escape from their gloomy reality. Athletic young men are fleeing the desperation of living in Gaza by combining crude martial arts and terrifying gymnastic manoeuvres. They’re unleashing their art—called Parkour or Free-running—on cemeteries, the skeletons of shelled buildings and dumpsites. What drives these adrenalin junkies to risk their lives and safety for a brief taste of freedom?


Script:


GAZA PARKOUR

SUPER CAPTION: KHAN YUNIS, GAZA



Location super "Khan Yunis, Gaza"

It’s a part of the world best known for its squalor, overcrowding and poverty.
For many, especially young people, Gaza is a cemetery of broken dreams.
But it’s precisely this depressing landscape that is giving hope to a new generation
Like twenty-year-old Abdullah Alqassab …
Each day he and his friends turn the Strip’s overcrowded pavements and sandy roads into their playground
For a few magical moments their bodies can soar as high as their dreams.

SOB: Abdullah Alqassab / Gaza Parkour (Arabic)
“When I practice Parkour I feel free as if I’m out of Gaza and I feel that I can overcome any difficulty in my life easily. Everything in this sport is easy. You can overcome barriers and hurdles easily and quickly. Everywhere I go I practice Parkour.”

SOB: Ahmed Matar / Gaza Parkour (Arabic)
“I practice Parkour because it's a dangerous sport and I personally love doing adventurous things and it's known about me since I was a child that I was energetic like a monkey.”

Invented in France in the 1990s, Parkour – or ‘freerunning’ as it’s sometimes called - has evolved from a military training programme for French Special Forces into a hugely popular extreme sport.
Abdullah and his friend Ahmed have been practicing it since they were ten years old and are the local champs.

SOB: Ahmed Matar / Gaza Parkour (Arabic)
“In the beginning I practiced Kung Fu in a club where I knew the guys and they let me join their team. We were 20 members and we created the first (Parkour) team in Palestine and in the Arab world. After that, many Arab teams were created too.”

SOB: Abdullah Alqassab / Gaza Parkour (Arabic)
“In the beginning we faced some obstacles as people couldn’t accept this sport because it’s very dangerous and they think it’s similar to monkeys’ movements so it was not popular in Gaza. But after sharing videos of us while we practiced, it opened doors to training people and the number of people interested in this sport increased.”

After his morning university classes are over, Abdullah gets ready for five hours of daily practice
He’s studying to become a translator but knows his chances of finding work in Gaza are bleak
His friend Ahmed finished school last year and is still unemployed.
According to the World Bank, as many as 44% of Gazans are jobless – one of the highest rates in the world
Which is why for the new generation of Gaza, Parkour is more than a sport – it’s the ultimate escape from reality.
They’ve yet to compete on the international stage as traveling abroad is complicated.

SOB: Ahmed Matar / Gaza Parkour (Arabic)
“We personally received many invitations from many countries to participate in international events and competitions. We even talked to the founder of Parkour but we couldn't participate because of the crossing closures.”

And there are more obstacles the team has to overcome
Gaza is one of the most densely populated areas in the world
Which means there’re few open spaces
And certainly no tailor-made buildings or gyms to practice the sport, like elsewhere in the world.

SOB: Abdullah Alqassab / Gaza Parkour (Arabic)
“We do it where there are demolitions and at cemeteries as they are the only places that have hurdles, walls and other things needed to do this sport.”

Buildings destroyed in the various conflicts with Israel are also ideal for practicing.
But the risks are huge.
A few weeks ago a team member, Mohammed Zaqout, fell while trying a new maneuver – and he’s still in intensive care.
A somber reminder of just how dangerous the sport is.

SOB: Abdullah Alqassab / Gaza Parkour (Arabic)
“I consider all the team's members as my brothers. I almost died of fright when he fell down from the fifth floor. But he miraculously survived thanks to God. He is really like my brother so I can't describe my feelings at that time accurately.”

But what the youngsters can accurately describe is the thrill of freedom and pulse of adrenaline that spurs them on to take even greater risks
What others see as death defying they’ll continue to see as life affirming.

SOB: Abdullah Alqassab / Gaza Parkour (Arabic)
“You do it knowing that you may fall at any moment and we have already fallen many times and stayed in hospital for days, but we came back to practice again because this will not stop us and will only strengthen our determination. It's planted in our blood.”

1) Plays out before the show, 'coming up tonight on CB' promo : 15 seconds
"Young men trapped in a war-torn Gaza Strip defy the odds - and death itself - through free-running or Parkour.
UP SOUND = 8 secs. "I feel free as if I'm out of Gaza and I feel that I can overcome any difficulty in my life."

2) Plays out before the show, "coming up tonight on CB' promo : 15 seconds
"It's the ultimate escape from reality. Young men flee the desperation of Gaza by practicing crude martial arts and terrifying gymnastic manoeuvres in cemeteries, shelled buildings and dumpsites. What drives these adrenalin junkies to risk their lives?

3) Play out during the show after a 'coming up next' : 10 seconds
For many young people Gaza is a cemetery of broken dreams. But this depressing landscape has given hope to teens whose death-defying stunts offer the ultimate escape."
